prospect.name: Erim
prospect.occupation: Desk-based, works in front of a computer all day and runs between meetings
prospect.training_background: Runner for 12-13 years plus daily walking. Gym-trained before ~2011-2012, then quit because he found it boring. Occasional home dumbbell work with no consistency. Currently no strength training at all.
prospect.age_note: Exact age not stated. Said 'I'll be 40 soon' and 'your 30s are over and you're approaching 40s'.
prospect.medical_note: No conditions, injuries or medications disclosed. Explicitly denies injury history: 'No, not really. No injuries.'

signals: Anchored hard and repeatedly to a much lower price: 'the range I would be comfortable with is maybe $300, $400, maximum $500, but I don't think I will go up to $1,000 a month'
Self-directed and confident he could do it alone: 'if I trained myself, and I could very well spend $6,000 on a power rack, and work out for a year... I don't need Trevor for that transformation'
Demanded credentials rather than reassurance: 'what are Trevor's credentials, right? What has he done in the past academically?'
Note: he is also affluent ('it's a big investment, which, you know, I can afford'), so the resistance was to perceived value, not capacity to pay

goals.text: Get stronger for daily life, particularly a stronger back and shoulders to hold posture at a desk
Lose body fat and become leaner so the lower two abs become visible
Build muscle as a by-product rather than as a target
Build discipline so the routine survives long-term rather than lapsing after six months
Avoid injuring himself the way friends have with weightlifting and endurance sport
Eventually pass kettlebell training on to his children

pains.text: Weak back and poor posture from sitting at a computer all day
Finds gym training boring and isolated, which is why he stopped in ~2012 and never went back
Does not know how to hold or move a kettlebell and is afraid of injuring himself or dropping it on his foot
Has watched Trevor's content for months and bought nothing — no path from watching to doing
Does not want to count macros or be 'super hung up' on food

objections.raw_quote: I have to think about it.
objections.rep_response: Immediately isolated it — 'What is that mainly about? Is that mainly around the investment amount?' — which surfaced the real objection. Did not run the rest of the OA play.

objections.raw_quote: No, I think it's too much. $1,000 a month is too much.
objections.rep_response: Tested whether it was capacity or value, offered to 'split it up', and asked whether he saw the value. Never established value; the prospect held the position for the next fifteen minutes.

objections.raw_quote: if I trained myself, and I could very well spend $6,000 on a power rack, and work out for a year, or six months, and make that transformation myself, without needing Trevor
objections.rep_response: Turned his own earlier words back on him — 'didn't you just mention to me that buying a power rack isn't actually the thing that you should do because there's a big chance you will just stop with it again' — which the prospect conceded logically but did not act on.

objections.raw_quote: what are Trevor's credentials, right? What has he done in the past academically? ... what has he done in the past to request $1,000 a month from a potential client? And from me, from what I see, it's worth something, but it's not $1,000.
objections.rep_response: Did not answer. Offered no credentials, no client references and no track record beyond 'You have seen that he can get the results, right?' Then pivoted straight to a cheaper product.

tiers.note: Primal University group programme quoted at $200 per month, cancellable monthly — offered as a downsell after the $6,000 was refused

offer.payment_plan_terms: Rep said 'We could split it up if that makes it better' and 'In the amount of payments that's needed' but never proposed a number of instalments, an amount or a total.

evidence: Explicit and repeated refusal of the offer on value, not affordability: 'I'm not going to spend $6,000 without seeing what he offers me and what results I'm getting. I'm not going to do that.'
'the range I would be comfortable with is maybe $300, $400, maximum $500, but I don't think I will go up to $1,000 a month'
'No, I'm not questioning the worth. I'm questioning what I will be getting out of the $6,000.'

Counter-evidence: he did verbally accept a $200/month downsell and a link was sent in the chat — 'Yeah, yeah, let's do that. That sounds more reasonable' and 'Now this is reasonable, Richard' — but he did not complete signup on the call ('Let me go through this... And then I will definitely look at it and join') and the core offer was refused outright.
Rep booked a loose follow-up 'in a few months' rather than a next step on the $6,000 programme.
outcome.next_step: Prospect to join the $200/month Primal University community from the link sent in chat; rep to message him on his work number in a couple of hours and revisit the one-to-one programme in a few months.

notable.note: The clearest value-objection in the batch and the one the script has no answer for. Erim explicitly said money was not the barrier ('it's a big investment, which, you know, I can afford') and asked twice for Trevor's credentials — the one question that would have closed him — and was never given an answer. The rep instead dropped from $6,000 to a $200/month community product inside four minutes of the objection landing. The rep also created time pressure at the moment of the downsell: 'let me just quickly text someone, because I'm actually late for another meeting.'

quality.notes: Frequent short-turn inversion, and several whole rep passages are attributed to 'Erim' — e.g. the discovery questions at 00:04:40, 00:26:36 and 00:52:57 are labelled as the prospect. The core exchanges (price, objection, downsell) are unambiguous from content.
